```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load packages
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

# Set seed
set.seed(2)
```

## Learning Objectives

- Create a Kaplan-Meier curve.
- Interpret a Kaplan-Meier curve.
- Define, use, and interpret median survival.

## Lesson

```{r}
# Parameters
n <- 100
t_median <- 5
lambda <- log(2) / t_median

# Generate data
t_survival <- rexp(n = n,
                   rate = lambda)
t_censor <- rexp(n = n,
                 rate = lambda)
t_censor[t_censor > 10] <- 10
d_survival <- data.frame(time = pmin(t_survival,
                                     t_censor),
                         death = as.integer(t_survival <= t_censor))
```

Suppose we run a study where we recruit 100 people with a serious disease
and measure time from diagnosis until death.
We only have the money to run the study for ten years,
so any participant who is still alive after ten years is automatically
censored at that time.
Some participants drop out or are lost to follow-up for other reasons,
leading to censoring.
These are the first ten rows of data:

```{r}
head(x = d_survival,
     n = 10)
```

The variable `time` is time from diagnosis to either death or censoring,
in years.
The variable `death` equals 1 for any participant whose time to death was
observed,
and 0 for any participant who was censored.
In this section we will learn how to display these data graphically,
in what's called a Kaplan-Meier curve.

The horizontal axis of the Kaplan-Meier curve is time from some origin.
It's very important that this axis label include (a) what that time origin is
and (b) what the units of time are.
The vertical axis is probability of survival,
i.e., $P(T > t)$, where $T$ is the time from the origin to the event.
The Kaplan-Meier curve always starts at the point $(0,1)$,
because at time zero, no one has had the event.

```{r}
# Have survival package work its magic
mod_01 <- survfit(Surv(time = time,
                       event = death) ~ 1,
                  data = d_survival)

# Empty plot
plot(x = 0,
     y = 1,
     xlim = c(0,10),
     ylim = c(0,1),
     xlab = "Years Since Diagnosis",
     ylab = "Probability of Survival",
     pch = 19)
```

Where do we go from here?
Moving from left to right,
the curve will remain constant until there is at least one event.
When there is at least one event, the curve will drop.
The trick is figuring out how much the curve should drop.

In order to explain the next steps,
I need to use some new notation.
To be consistent with the example, I'm going to use "death" and "event"
interchangeably.
Also, I'm going to assume the deaths all happened at different times.
Define the following:

- $k$ is the index for the deaths.
So, $k = 1$ indicates the first death,
$k = 2$ indicates the second death,
and so forth.
- $t_k$ is the time of the $k$th death.
- $N_k$ is the number of people at risk at time $t_k$.
In other words, $N_k$ is the number of people who have neither died
nor been censored before $t_k$.
- $D_k$ is the number of deaths at $t_k$.
Since we're assuming that all the deaths happened at unique times,
$D_k$ will just be 1 for each $k$.

In order to make our Kaplan-Meier curve,
we are going to fill in the following table:

| $k$ | $t_k$ | $N_k$ | $D_k$ | $\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k)$ |
|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|
| 0 | 0 | | | | | 1 |

How do we get those last three columns?

- $\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)$ is an estimate of the probability
that the death happens exactly at $t_k$, given that it hasn't happened
before $t_k$.
This is fairly straightforward to compute:
We will divide the number of deaths at $t_k$ by the number of people
at risk at $t_k$.
In symbols,
$$
\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k) = \frac{D_k}{N_k} \text{.}
$$
- $\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)$ is an estimate of the probability
that the death happens after $t_k$, i.e., that someone survives past $t_k$,
given that the death didn't happen before $t_k$.
This is
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_k | T \ge t_k) \\
&= 1 - \frac{D_k}{N_k} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
$$
- $\hat{P}(T > t_k)$ is what we actually want to plot;
unfortunately, it's the least straightforward quantity to compute.
We use the following logic:
$$
\begin{align}
\hat{P}(T > t_k) &= \hat{P}(T > t_k, T \ge t_{k}) \\
&= \hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_{k}) \hat{P}(T \ge t_{k}) \\
&= \hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_{k}) \hat{P}(T > t_{k-1}) \text{.}
\end{align}
$$

Let's start filling in the table.
In order to do so, we must first sort our data set from smallest to largest
time.

```{r}
head(x = d_survival[order(d_survival$time), ],
     n = 10)
```

Note that $t_1 = 0.02841937$.
At the time of the first death,
no one has been censored, so there are 100 people at risk.
There's exactly one death at $t_1$,
so
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T = t_1|T \ge t_1) &= \frac{D_1}{N_1} \\
&= \frac{1}{100} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_1 | T \ge t_1) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_1|T \ge t_1) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{100} \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_1) &= \hat{P}(T > t_1 | T \ge t_{1}) \hat{P}(T > t_{0}) \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \times 1 \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$


| $k$ | $t_k$ | $N_k$ | $D_k$ | $\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k)$ |
|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|
| 0 | 0 | | | | | 1 |
| 1 | 0.02841937 | 100 | 1 | 0.01 | 0.99 | 0.99 |

Moving on,
we have $t_2 = 0.11406225$.
At the time of the second death,
three people have been censored and one has already died, so there are 96 people at risk.
There's exactly one death at $t_2$,
so
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T = t_2|T \ge t_2) &= \frac{D_2}{N_2} \\
&= \frac{1}{96} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_2 | T \ge t_2) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_2|T \ge t_2) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{96} \\
&= \frac{95}{96} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_2) &= \hat{P}(T > t_2 | T \ge t_{2}) \hat{P}(T > t_{1}) \\
&= \frac{95}{96} \times \frac{99}{100} \times 1 \\
&\approx 0.9796875 \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$


| $k$ | $t_k$ | $N_k$ | $D_k$ | $\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k)$ |
|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|
| 0 | 0 | | | | | 1 |
| 1 | 0.02841937 | 100 | 1 | 0.01000000 | 0.9900000 | 0.9900000 |
| 2 | 0.11406225 | 96 | 1 | 0.01041667 | 0.9895833 | 0.9796875 |

Let's do one more and then have R take over.
We have $t_3 = 0.22482600	$.
At the time of the third death,
three people have been censored and two have already died, so there are 95 people at risk.
There's exactly one death at $t_3$,
so
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T = t_3|T \ge t_3) &= \frac{D_3}{N_3} \\
&= \frac{1}{95} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_3 | T \ge t_3) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_3|T \ge t_3) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{95} \\
&= \frac{94}{95} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_3) &= \hat{P}(T > t_3 | T \ge t_{3}) \hat{P}(T > t_{2}) \\
&= \frac{94}{95} \times \frac{95}{96} \times \frac{99}{100} \times 1 \\
&\approx 0.969375 \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$


| $k$ | $t_k$ | $N_k$ | $D_k$ | $\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)$ | $\hat{P}(T > t_k)$ |
|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|-:|
| 0 | 0 | | | | | 1 |
| 1 | 0.02841937 | 100 | 1 | 0.01000000 | 0.9900000 | 0.9900000 |
| 2 | 0.11406225 | 96 | 1 | 0.01041667 | 0.9895833 | 0.9796875 |
| 3 | 0.22482600 | 95 | 1 | 0.01052632 | 0.9894737 | 0.9693750 |


Instead of doing this 48 more times, let's have R plot
the Kaplan-Meier curve for us.
We can use base R or the package `ggsurvfit` to make the plot.
Either way, we need the package `survival`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Have survival package work its magic
mod_01 <- survfit(Surv(time = time,
                       event = death) ~ 1,
                  data = d_survival)

# Base R plotting
plot(x = mod_01,
     xlab = "Years Since Diagnosis",
     ylab = "Probability of Survival")

# ggsurvfit plotting
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = time,
                        event = death) ~ 1,
                   data = d_survival)) +
  labs(x = "Years Since Diagnosis",
       y = "Probability of Survival")
```

Ta-da! Now we have an estimate of $P(T > t)$ for each value of $t$
from 0 to 10.

There's one more term we have to learn, which is "median survival".
Median survival is the time $t_{0.5}$ such that $P(T > t_{0.5}) = 0.5$,
i.e., the time that we would expect approximately half the people to survive
past.
It's very easy to get median survival from the `survfit` object:
```{r}
mod_01
```
As we can see, the median survival is 5.98.
So, people have a 50\% chance of surviving past 5.98 years after their diagnosis.

On the Kaplan-Meier curve, the median survival is the point on the horizontal
axis where the height of the curve is 0.5.
```{r}
# Base R plotting
plot(x = mod_01,
     xlab = "Years Since Diagnosis",
     ylab = "Probability of Survival")
abline(h = 0.5,
       v = 5.98)

# ggsurvfit plotting
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = time,
                        event = death) ~ 1,
                   data = d_survival)) +
  labs(x = "Years Since Diagnosis",
       y = "Probability of Survival") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5.98)
```
